evidence.finding: Mean AHT rose from 375.2 seconds before 09:15 to 524.2 seconds from 09:15 onward, an increase of 149.0 seconds (39.7%); the window maximum was 573.7 seconds.
Mean service level fell from 86.7% before the incident to 60.4% afterward, a decline of 26.3 percentage points.
Mean ASA increased from 30.6 seconds to 65.3 seconds after the incident, a 113.3% increase.
Mean offered calls were essentially stable across the boundary, moving from 81.0 to 78.9 calls per interval (-2.6%), which does not support a demand spike.
No operational events were visible during the evaluation window.

primary_root_cause_detail: A sustained post-incident increase in average handle time appears to have reduced throughput and driven the service-level deterioration; demand did not increase across the incident boundary.
recommended_actions: Identify the call types, workflows, or agent cohorts responsible for the AHT increase beginning at 09:15.
Review interval-level transfer rates and queue results to determine whether transfers or localized work mix drove longer handling.
Implement real-time AHT alerts and intraday capacity actions when handle time materially exceeds plan.
Validate that staffing and adherence remained adequate before closing the incident review.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Offered calls decreased slightly after the incident boundary rather than surging.
No platform or other operational event was recorded in the visible event data.

stakeholder_summary: CC-003 was most likely caused by a sustained handle-time increase beginning at the incident boundary. AHT rose about 40%, while offered demand remained stable; service level fell 26.3 points and ASA more than doubled. No visible event supports a platform explanation. Staffing and queue-level validation would further strengthen attribution.
